exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio of a Quadrantal Angle Greater Than One Full Rotation

question.explanation:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $4\pi$ that lies in the range $[0, 2\pi).$ \begin{align} 4\pi - 2\pi &= 2\pi\\[3pt] 2\pi - 2\pi &= 0\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align}

Therefore, $\sec{0} = \sec{4\pi}.$

The angle $0$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos{0} = 1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\sec{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta},$ we have \[ \sec{0} = \dfrac{1}{\cos{0} } = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1. \]

Therefore, $\sec{0} = 1.$

example.title: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio of a Quadrantal Angle Greater Than One Full Rotation

question.explanation:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\dfrac{11\pi}{2}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi).$

\begin{align} \dfrac{11\pi}{2} - 2\pi &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\\[5pt] \dfrac{7\pi}{2} - 2\pi &= \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align}

Therefore, $\sin\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{2}\right)= \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right).$

The angle $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1.$

Therefore, $\sin \left(\dfrac{11\pi}{2}\right) = -1.$

example.title: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio of a Quadrantal Angle Greater Than One Full Rotation

question.explanation:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\dfrac{9\pi}{2}$ that lies in the range $[0, 2\pi).$

\begin{align} \dfrac{9\pi}{2} - 2\pi &= \dfrac{5\pi}{2}\\[5pt] \dfrac{5\pi}{2} - 2\pi &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align}

Therefore, $\cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cot\left(\dfrac{9\pi}{2}\right).$

The angle $90^\circ$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0.$

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\cot{\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ we have \[ \cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{0}{1} = 0. \]

Therefore, $\cot\left(\dfrac{9\pi}{2}\right) = 0.$

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Trigonometric Ratio of a Negative Quadrantal Angle

question.explanation:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ that lies in the range $[0, 2\pi).$ \begin{align} -\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + 2\pi & = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align}

Therefore, $\cos\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$

The angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)= 0.$

Therefore, $\cos\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 0.$

example.title: Computing the Trigonometric Ratio of a Negative Quadrantal Angle

question.explanation:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-90^\circ$ that lies in the range $[0,360^\circ).$

\[ -90^\circ + 360^\circ = 270^\circ\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \]

Therefore, $\csc \left(-90^\circ \right) = \csc \left(270^\circ\right).$

The angle $270^\circ$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $270^\circ$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left(270^\circ\right) = -1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\csc{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have

\[ \csc \left(270^\circ \right) = \dfrac{1}{\sin{\left(270^\circ \right) }} = \dfrac{1}{-1} = -1. \]

Therefore, $\csc \left(-90^\circ \right) = -1.$
